junction.name: Delancey Street & Essex Street, New York City

claims.text: Delancey Street & Essex Street had 104 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 32 pedestrians injured, 28 cyclists injured and 0 people killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $7.1 million a year.
50% of crashes here happened at night (7 pm to 6 am), against 36% at the city's priority junctions.
18% of crashes here involved a taxi or for-hire car, against 6% at the city's priority junctions.

Held up on later years: no one hurt and a taxi or for-hire car was involved in 13% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 3% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search and the exhaustive search).

Held up on later years: a vehicle was going straight ahead and a taxi or for-hire car was involved in 14% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 4% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search and the exhaustive search).

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: passed the causal gate (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).

Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 3.1 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $1.1 million a year; check on site: an entry on yellow or red.

Yellow Change Intervals would avoid about 1.6 crashes a year (CMF 4219, the more conservative of the two middle records of 4; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $556,000 a year; check on site: an entry on yellow or red; the current yellow plus all-red time is below the ITE recommended practice.
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for Delancey Street, Essex Street (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 1, New York City Council; Manhattan Community Board 3.
A request letter to the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is drafted and checked.

draft_request.letter:
To: the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
Cc: Council Member, District 1, New York City Council; Manhattan Community Board 3
Subject: Subject: Request for safety study at Delancey Street & Essex Street

Dear colleagues at NYC DOT,

Over the 5 years from 31 October 2021, the official record for Delancey Street & Essex Street shows 251 crashes, including 104 injury crashes. In those crashes 32 pedestrians and 28 cyclists were injured. No one was killed. The harm is valued at $7.1 million per year in the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars). This junction is a City priority location. No safety work is recorded here in the 5-year period, though a Leading Pedestrian Interval signal is recorded here from 2008.

We ask you to carry out a safety study for the roads you are responsible for – Delancey Street and Essex Street – and to implement fixes where site checks confirm they are suitable.

Longer yellow signal times could prevent injury crashes where an entry on yellow or red is confirmed on site, with about 5.7 crashes avoided per year and about $1,937,000 in harm avoided per year.

Reflective backplates on the traffic signals could prevent injury crashes where an entry on yellow or red is confirmed on site, with about 3.1 crashes avoided per year and about $1,068,000 in harm avoided per year.

Please let us know the outcome of the study and the actions planned on your network.

Yours sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]

- NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (corridors); NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (intersections); NYC Vision Zero View, Enhanced Crossings (6ax4-q5k4); NYC Vision Zero View, Leading Pedestrian Interval Signals; NYC Vision Zero View, Signal Timing/25 MPH Retiming; NYC Vision Zero View, Speed Humps (jknp-skuy); NYC Vision Zero View, Turn Traffic Calming; NYC Vision Zero priority corridors; NYC Vision Zero priority intersections
- FHWA CMF Clearinghouse, CMF 4215 (longer yellow signal times)
